title: Mental Health Prediction Using Machine Learning
summary: An MSc research project exploring machine-learning approaches to predicting student mental-health risk from academic and behavioural data.
question: How can machine-learning methods be evaluated for identifying patterns associated with student mental-health risk?
approach: Document the dataset provenance, preprocessing decisions, train/validation/test design, candidate models, evaluation metrics and limitations. The original portfolio describes this as the MSc thesis; exact results should be added only after checking the dissertation and code.
lessons: This project is a useful starting point for discussing data quality, responsible use of sensitive data, model evaluation and the difference between predictive performance and real-world clinical usefulness.

title: EMNIST Character Classification
summary: A neural-network project using the EMNIST dataset to explore handwritten character classification and compare multilayer perceptron and convolutional approaches.
question: How does model architecture affect character-classification performance?
approach: Rebuild the notebook/script as a reproducible experiment: state the dataset split, preprocessing, model definitions, training setup, random seed and per-class evaluation.
lessons: Compare a simple baseline with a CNN, inspect a confusion matrix and analyse errors rather than reporting accuracy alone.

title: Semantic Segmentation
summary: A semantic-segmentation assignment using the Cambridge Labeled Objects in Video dataset, described in the original portfolio as 101 images with pixel-level labels across 32 object classes.
question: Can a deep-learning model assign a semantic class to each pixel in a scene?
approach: Record the train/validation split, image and mask transformations, loss function, baseline, and segmentation metrics such as mean Intersection over Union (mIoU).
lessons: Segmentation requires careful handling of class imbalance, image-mask alignment and metrics that reflect pixel-level overlap.

title: Multi-Armed Bandit Algorithms
summary: An implementation-focused assignment on n-armed bandits, inspired by Sutton and Barto's Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.
question: How do different action-selection strategies balance exploration and exploitation?
approach: Create a repeatable simulation over many random seeds and compare reward over time, cumulative regret and sensitivity to algorithm parameters.
lessons: Average results across runs and include uncertainty; a single reward curve can be misleading.

title: OpenAI Gym / Gymnasium Environment
summary: A project exploring a deep-reinforcement-learning method in a Gym-style environment.
question: Can an agent learn a useful policy through interaction with an environment?
approach: Name the environment and algorithm, document reward design and hyperparameters, compare against a random or simple baseline, and show learning curves across independent seeds.
lessons: Reward design, environment versions and evaluation protocols strongly affect reproducibility.

title: Natural Language Processing — Multilingual Chatbot Concept
summary: A research project proposing a multilingual chatbot system for business-to-business and business-to-consumer use, including translation support.
question: How could multilingual conversational support be designed for users with different language needs?
approach: Present this as a design/research project unless a working implementation can be demonstrated. Add architecture, language coverage, test cases and evaluation evidence where available.
lessons: A credible NLP portfolio distinguishes a proposed design from a tested system and measures translation quality and task completion.

title: Binary Classification Model Comparison
summary: An applied-AI assignment comparing supervised-learning methods on a binary-classification problem.
question: How do different supervised methods compare under the same evaluation protocol?
approach: Identify the dataset and algorithms from the original submission, use a leakage-safe split, compare precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC where appropriate, and discuss threshold choice.
lessons: Model comparisons are only meaningful when preprocessing and validation are consistent across models.

title: Clustering Word Embeddings
summary: A clustering assignment involving words represented by 300-dimensional embedding vectors.
question: What structure can clustering reveal in a space of word embeddings?
approach: Document scaling or normalization choices, compare clustering methods, use suitable internal metrics, and inspect representative words from clusters. Avoid claiming semantic quality from a score alone.
lessons: High-dimensional distance measures and the choice of cluster count can substantially affect interpretation.

title: Voting Rules
summary: A Python assignment implementing voting rules over agent preference orderings and alternatives.
question: How do different voting rules aggregate individual preference rankings into a collective outcome?
approach: Explain the input representation, each implemented rule, tie handling and test cases. Include small examples that make the outcomes easy to verify.
lessons: Clear tests and explicit edge-case handling are as important as the core algorithm.
status: Good candidate for a clean small repository

title: Bank Account Classes
summary: An object-oriented Python assignment implementing basic and premium bank-account classes.
question: How can inheritance and class design represent account behaviour while preserving clear invariants?
approach: Document the class API, validation rules, transaction behaviour and tests for normal and invalid operations.
lessons: Encapsulation, precise method contracts and unit tests make small projects easier to maintain.
status: Good candidate for a clean small repository
